Code Defect: Before removing an export from a shared infrastructure module (e.g., `preview/globals`, `manager/globals`, or any `definitions`/`globals` barrel), verify the export is not imported anywhere in the monorepo—including builder packages and other lib packages—and confirm with teammates that no in-progress work depends on it; if uncertain, keep the export and add a TODO comment rather than deleting it.

When migrating addon `package.json` entries from `peerDependencies` to `devDependencies`, audit each package's actual import usage in the addon's source files before including it as a devDependency; do not mechanically carry over every previous peer dep—remove packages (e.g., `react-dom`) that are not directly imported by the addon's own source.
Avoid using CSS properties or values with limited browser support (e.g., `white-space: balance`) in styled components; prefer well-supported alternatives (e.g., `white-space: normal`) instead.
Remove all `console.log` statements before merging; debug logging must not appear in committed, production-bound code.

Do not merge code with unresolved TODO or FIXME comments for functionality intended to be part of the same change; conversely, remove any FIXME/TODO comments whose described issue has already been resolved by the PR—leftover resolved-issue annotations are misleading. Either resolve the TODO, convert it to a tracked issue, or delete it if already addressed.

Avoid bypassing TypeScript's type system via `as any` casts, unverified `as SomeType` assertions, or `@ts-expect-error` suppressions. Instead, fix the underlying type definitions to accurately reflect runtime values, use typed type-guard functions to narrow discriminated unions, and add runtime structural guards (e.g., `'prop' in obj` plus `Array.isArray()`) before narrowing or casting. A `@ts-expect-error` on a code path is often a signal that the type definitions need correction, not that the error should be silenced.
Do not add defensive optional chaining (e.g., `prop?.method()`) on props that are typed as required and non-nullable; unnecessary guards add noise and can mask genuine type mismatches.

When a preset hook's return type doesn't match the expected signature from `PresetProperty<T>`, fix the type definition of `PresetProperty<T>` rather than casting the return value to `never` at the call site. Casting `as never` tells TypeScript the value is impossible, silently suppressing type errors and masking the real mismatch.

When forwarding any optional property from `options.angularBuilderOptions` into `builderOptions` in `framework-preset-angular-cli.ts`, always guard the assignment with an `!== undefined` check (e.g., `if (options.angularBuilderOptions?.prop !== undefined) { builderOptions.prop = options.angularBuilderOptions.prop; }`). An unconditional optional-chain assignment will overwrite an already-merged default with `undefined` whenever the caller omits that option.

In documentation code examples (e.g., package.json script blocks, config file snippets, CSS/JSX/MDX), verify that all entries are syntactically complete, unique, and technically correct: no duplicate keys, no incomplete template tokens (e.g., `<project-name` missing its closing `>`), CSS numeric values must include units (e.g., `min-height: 40px` not `min-height: 40`), and code blocks must be free of stray or extraneous characters (e.g., trailing semicolons after JSX/MDX closing tags).

Before merging MDX documentation that uses custom JSX components or references static asset paths (e.g., icon image URLs), confirm the components are implemented/exported and the asset files exist in the repository or are served by the build pipeline. Missing components silently break rendering; missing assets should be added or paths corrected consistently across all pages.

When writing a test for a concurrency/race-condition fix, ensure the test would actually fail without the fix: (1) wrap the promise under test to track a boolean `resolved` flag, (2) assert `expect(resolved).toBe(false)` after a short `setTimeout` wait but *before* releasing any blocking gate, and (3) verify that mock stubs don't inadvertently allow the awaited operation to complete early.

When calling functions that search for a descendant and may legitimately return `null`/`undefined` (e.g., `findLeafEntry` when all children are filtered out), always capture the return value and guard with a truthiness check before passing it to consumers; silently no-op when nothing is found rather than risking a runtime error.

When updating MIGRATION.md with TypeScript configuration guidance, accurately state which `moduleResolution` modes (e.g., `bundler`, `nodenext`) reject extensionless imports and specify the exact setting required (e.g., `allowImportingTsExtensions`). Do not imply extensionless imports 'continue to work' without qualifying which tsconfig resolver supports them.

When a wrapper function or utility re-exposes a generic type parameter that corresponds to a specific third-party interface (e.g., Vue's `App<HostElement>`), match that interface's own default type exactly rather than substituting a seemingly stricter alternative; diverging from upstream defaults (e.g., replacing `= any` with `= Element`) can cause type incompatibilities for callers who rely on the upstream contract.

When documentation prose names a specific version of an external tool and links to that tool's versioned documentation site, confirm that the URL's version identifier matches the version stated in the text (e.g., a reference to 'Vite 5' must link to v5.vite.dev, not v6.vite.dev).

Code examples that demonstrate package imports should use the canonical import path given in the upstream library's official documentation; do not add explicit file extensions to import specifiers when the official docs omit them (e.g., `require('next/jest')` is preferred over `require('next/jest.js')`).

When narrowing a discriminated-union variant (e.g., `TSType`) by its `name` string, also investigate whether a structural property unique to that variant (e.g., the presence or absence of `raw`, or the shape of `value`) can serve as a more robust discriminant; verify that the chosen structural property is consistent across all runtime inputs before relying on it as a type guard.

When an array property is tightened from optional (`prop?: T[]`) to required (`prop: T[]`), confirm that all runtime code paths that construct or pass that object guarantee the property is present before calling array methods (`.filter()`, `.map()`, etc.) directly on it without optional chaining.

When a React component combines controlled state (`useState`) with a native `<details>` element, ensure the `<details>` is kept in sync via an `onToggle` handler (e.g., `onToggle={(e) => setState(e.currentTarget.open)}`). Relying solely on a React `onClick` to toggle state can cause desync when assistive technologies or browser features toggle the native `<details>` element outside React's event system.

Do not remove explicit `role="button"` from styled `<summary>` elements used as interactive toggles. Although `<summary>` has an implicit ARIA button role per spec, some browsers do not expose it to assistive technologies; the explicit attribute is required for consistent cross-browser AT support.

Storybook story files for interactive components (e.g., popovers, tooltips, expandable sections) must include a `play` function that programmatically exercises the interaction (opens the popover, expands the section, etc.), so the open/expanded state is captured in visual regression tests. Where both a minimal-content and a long/complex-content story variant exist, both should have play functions.

When using the `in` operator to duck-type a property before accessing it, also validate the property's runtime type—for example, add `Array.isArray(obj.prop)` before calling array methods such as `.length` or iterating, rather than relying on property existence alone.

When submitting a dependency version bump in `package.json` (and the accompanying lockfile update), verify that the target version actually exists on the npm registry before opening the PR (e.g., run `npm view <package> versions` or check the registry page); specifying a non-existent version will cause install and CI package-resolution to fail.

In `code/core/src/manager-api/modules/stories.ts`, whenever a defensive existence check is added or changed in one index-mutation function, audit all sibling functions (e.g., both `updateStory` and `updateDocs`) to ensure the same `if (index && index[id])` / `if (filteredIndex && filteredIndex[id])` guards are applied consistently in both the no-ref and ref branches before any mutation.

Changes to index-mutation functions in `code/core/src/manager-api/modules/stories.ts` (such as `updateStory` or `updateDocs`) must be tested for HMR regressions—verify that editing a story or docs entry still updates live in the Storybook UI without requiring a full page reload.

When augmenting a third-party TypeScript module's interface (e.g., augmenting `@emotion/react`'s `Theme` interface), always use `declare module 'the-third-party-package' { export interface Theme ... }` paired with a side-effect import of that package—never `declare module '.'`. A `declare module '.'` augmentation creates a new, local interface that does not merge with the third-party package's original interface; any code that imports `Theme` directly from the third-party package bypasses the augmentation entirely.

When reading a file to derive metadata needed for a subsequent write (e.g., reading `package.json` to detect indentation before rewriting it), wrap the read in a try/catch and return a sensible default on failure. This guards against cases where the target path does not yet exist or the file has moved.

When defaulting a value that could legitimately be `0` or another falsy number, use the nullish coalescing operator `??` rather than logical OR `||`. For example, `detectIndent(content).indent ?? 2` is correct; `|| 2` would incorrectly override a valid zero-width value.

When adding a new npm package import inside a monorepo workspace, verify that the package is declared in the `dependencies` (or `devDependencies`) of the specific workspace `package.json` that contains the importing file, not only at the repository root.

When a type needs to carry symbol-keyed metadata alongside strongly-typed string keys (e.g., extending a TypeFest-based type with internal Symbol metadata), use a symbol-only index signature `{ [k: symbol]: unknown }` rather than `Record<string | symbol, any>`. The latter widens all string-keyed properties to `any`, defeating the original type's guarantees.

Unit tests must import and directly invoke the real exported function under test rather than inlining equivalent logic inside the test body. Duplicating the implementation within the test means a regression in production code won't be detected—the test passes against its own copy of the logic. Ensure the function is exported from its module so the test can call and verify actual behavior.

When code in Storybook's Next.js framework packages (e.g., under `code/frameworks/nextjs/` or `code/frameworks/nextjs-vite/`) needs to import Next.js functionality—including in mock/export files and routing providers—use the public Next.js package entrypoints (e.g., `next/headers`, `next/navigation`, `next/router`) rather than internal `next/dist/*` paths. The `next/dist/*` paths are undocumented implementation details with no stability guarantees and can change across Next.js versions.

When story parameters are attached via the detached `StoryExport.parameters = { ... }` pattern (rather than inline inside the story object), verify that the variable name used in the assignment exactly matches the story export it is intended to configure—copy-paste errors can silently apply parameters to the wrong story while leaving the intended story unconfigured. This is especially common when converting stories from the legacy function-export style to CSF3 object style.

When calling `process.exit()` on an error path (e.g., invalid user input, argument validation failure), always use a non-zero exit code such as `process.exit(1)`; using `process.exit(0)` on an error path incorrectly signals success to the calling shell or CI system.

When validating user-supplied arguments against a known list with a fuzzy-match/suggestion helper, treat every unrecognised argument as an error unconditionally—set the error flag and emit a descriptive error message even when the helper returns no close-match suggestion, rather than silently ignoring arguments for which no match is found.

When building URL query strings or path segments manually, prefer native `URLSearchParams` (which handles encoding automatically) over hand-rolled string concatenation; if manual construction is unavoidable, URL-encode every variable key and value with `encodeURIComponent` to prevent broken URLs from special characters.

Shortcut case handlers in `code/core/src/manager-api/modules/shortcuts.ts` that invoke story-dependent APIs (e.g., `fullAPI.getStoryHrefs`) must guard against `storyId` being `undefined` (possible on non-story pages such as About or Settings) with an explicit `if (!storyId) { break; }` before executing the action.

After verifying that a composed-ref entry (`refs[refId]`) exists, also check that `refs[refId].url` is a non-empty string before concatenating it to form a preview URL; skipping this check silently produces a URL like `'undefined/iframe.html'`.

Mock objects in `.stories.tsx` context fixtures must exactly match the actual API's property names and values—including correct key names (e.g., `managerHref`/`previewHref`, not `manager`/`preview`) and correct shortcut key casing—because mismatches cause stories and story-based tests to fail silently without type errors.

When splitting serialized `key:value` pairs (such as Storybook args or globals) with `.split(':')`, always pass a limit of `2` (i.e., `.split(':', 2)`) so that values which themselves contain colons (e.g., `theme:dark:blue` or `url:https://…`) are preserved in full rather than silently truncated.

When mocking Next.js (or other versioned framework) internal modules that were restructured between major versions, use dynamic `import()` wrapped in try/catch—following the pattern used in the webpack framework adapter—so the mock works across all supported framework versions rather than hard-coding a static import that fails in older versions.

When writing inline comments or JSDoc that reference environment variable names, verify that each name in the prose exactly matches the variable used in the surrounding code—the compiler will not catch a mismatch between a name in a comment and the actual variable (e.g., writing `BUILD_MODE` when the code uses `BUILD_TARGET`).

When looking up a value from a `Record`/map by a dynamic key (e.g., `filters[someKey].property`), always use optional chaining (`?.`) so that an unexpected or absent key does not throw at runtime; provide an explicit fallback value rather than relying on the key always being present.

When an effect hook injects a DOM element with a known ID via `insertAdjacentHTML` or similar, first check `document.getElementById(id)` and skip insertion if the element already exists, preventing duplicates when multiple component instances mount. In the corresponding cleanup, retrieve the element with `getElementById` and guard the removal with an existence check (e.g., `element?.parentNode?.removeChild(element)`) rather than a non-null assertion, so the cleanup does not throw if the element was already removed by other code.

When a helper called inside a `useEffect` body returns a cleanup/teardown function, capture that return value and invoke it inside the `useEffect`'s own cleanup callback; silently discarding it means teardown logic (e.g., restoring a DOM style property) never runs when the effect re-fires or the component unmounts.

Do not parse a CSS `filter` property value by splitting on whitespace—filter functions such as `drop-shadow(2px 2px 4px black)` contain spaces within their arguments and will be fragmented incorrectly. Instead, save the entire original filter string before modification and restore it verbatim in cleanup, or use a regex that matches complete filter function tokens.

TypeScript triple-slash directives (`/// <reference types="..." />`) must not be followed by a trailing semicolon; the semicolon causes TypeScript to treat the line as an ordinary comment rather than a directive.

When writing a dynamic `import()` expression for a third-party package, verify whether the target symbol is a default export or a named export before deciding on import syntax. CommonJS-compiled packages frequently expose their main class only as a default export; destructuring `{ SymbolName }` from such a module yields `undefined` at runtime. If the package uses a default export, access it as `(await import('pkg')).default`.

Before adding `import type { SomeName }` from an external package, confirm that `SomeName` is actually present in that package's published type declarations (`.d.ts` files or re-exports). If the package does not export the expected type by name, define the interface locally—for example via `ConstructorParameters<typeof ThePlugin>[0]` or a hand-written interface—rather than importing a non-existent named type.

When writing GitHub Actions conditions to detect or skip fork PRs, use `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork != true` rather than comparing `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository`. The `full_name` comparison can silently misbehave when `head.repo` is null (e.g., the originating fork was later deleted), while the boolean `fork` property is the purpose-built, null-safe alternative. This pattern is already established in `trigger-circle-ci-workflow.yml` and should be used consistently across all workflow files.
Unit tests for URL-building functions must include cases for special characters in parameter values (e.g., `=`, `&`, `;`, `:` within a value) to verify that encoding is applied correctly end-to-end.
Maintainability and Readability: When destructuring an array to skip leading elements, use an empty slot (e.g., `const [, value] = arr`) rather than a throwaway `_` variable. Named-but-unused `_`-prefixed bindings can trigger the project's `@typescript-eslint/naming-convention` lint rule. Default values can be applied in the same pattern (e.g., `const [, value = []] = arr`).

When migration docs or other documentation links to external code examples, consider whether to link to the final file on the default branch or to a PR diff. Link to a PR diff when the purpose is to show readers what changes to make; if so, ensure the surrounding prose makes it explicit so readers know to follow the diff pattern.

Use meaningful, descriptive `id` and `className` values on DOM elements; avoid placeholder names (e.g., `figure-out-id`) and legacy or ambiguous class names that no longer clearly describe the element's role.

Extract repeated or non-obvious magic values (pixel sizes, durations, numeric defaults) into named constants or CSS variables rather than inlining them at multiple sites, so future changes require updating only one place.

Use specific, user-facing text for initial or default UI states rather than vague placeholders; a label that clearly communicates what has not yet occurred is easier to understand at a glance than a generic 'not yet' phrase.

When using non-obvious encodings in source code (e.g., a two-digit hex suffix for alpha opacity like `#aabbcc22`), add a brief inline comment explaining the encoding so future readers do not have to decode it.

On framework-specific documentation pages, verify that all prose references to the framework name (builder, renderer, etc.) match the page's actual subject. Copy-pasting from a sibling page commonly introduces incorrect framework name references.

The opening sentence of the Install section in `docs/get-started/frameworks/*.mdx` pages should follow the canonical phrasing: "To install Storybook in an existing [Framework] project, run this command in your project's root directory."

When editing framework documentation pages, check for and remove any content—migration callouts, configuration notes, or version-specific guidance—that applies only to Storybook major versions that are no longer supported or relevant to current users.

Keep PRs strictly scoped to their stated objective. Verify that every changed file is traceable to the PR's purpose; flag any unrelated changes and request extraction into a separate, focused pull request with its own description, tests, and documentation. In dependency-upgrade PRs specifically, flag any source or configuration changes that go beyond package manifest updates and mechanical API-migration fixes (e.g., renamed types, updated call signatures); ask the author to confirm each such change is intentional and explain why it is part of the upgrade.

In Vitest test files, place mock setup (`vi.mocked(...)`, `vi.spyOn(...)`, `mockImplementationOnce`, `mockResolvedValueOnce`, etc.) in `beforeEach` blocks rather than inline within individual `it`/`test` bodies. Call `vi.clearAllMocks()` in `beforeEach` or `afterEach` to prevent cross-test state leakage.

When adding non-obvious filtering or defensive logic that compensates for stale persisted state (e.g., `shortcutKeys` entries from localStorage never registered in the current session), include an inline comment explaining *why* the filtering is required—not just what it does.

Add JSDoc (`/** */` block comments, not `/* */`) to every exported utility function in framework and shared packages (e.g., under `code/frameworks/`), documenting the function's purpose, each parameter, and the full range of return values—including graceful-failure paths (e.g., 'returns `false` when the version string cannot be coerced by semver'). Use `/** */` syntax so IDE hover tooltips are populated. Mark deprecated exports with the `@deprecated` JSDoc tag naming the replacement, e.g., `@deprecated Use api.getStoryHrefs from storybook/manager-api`.

When an API's configuration already constrains its callback arguments (e.g., `MutationObserver` with `attributeFilter`, or a typed event handler), do not add redundant `forEach` loops, `if` checks, or other guards that re-verify the guaranteed constraint; the extra code adds noise without safety.

Add explanatory inline or JSDoc comments to code that implements non-obvious workarounds (e.g., browser quirks, framework-specific issues like React.StrictMode, cross-frame communication). The comment should describe the problem being solved, the specific runtime conditions or environment under which it occurs, and where applicable link to the relevant spec issue or browser bug, so future maintainers can reason about scope and continued necessity.
Always reference channel event names via their exported named constants from `storybook/internal/core-events`; never use inline magic strings for event names in `emit`/`on` calls.

Name event constants (e.g., in `core-events`) after the semantic purpose or behavioral contract they establish for consumers—what they should do or what state has changed—rather than the low-level browser mechanism that triggers them (e.g., prefer `FOCUS_TRAP_CHANGE` over `INERT_ATTRIBUTE_CHANGED`).

When editing MIGRATION.md, verify that no explanatory paragraph or sentence is accidentally duplicated within or across sections; each breaking-change or deprecation notice should appear exactly once.

When documenting or writing `yarn task` commands (in READMEs, instructions, AI-assistant guidance, etc.), always include the `--start-from` flag (e.g., `--start-from auto`) to prevent the CLI from entering interactive mode and blocking in non-interactive contexts such as CI or agent sessions. Use `yarn task` as the primary documented command form (the project's canonical task-runner wrapper); if raw `yarn nx` equivalents are shown, present them as alternatives alongside the `yarn task` form.

When attaching module-private metadata to objects (e.g., indentation style on a parsed `package.json`), define a module-level `Symbol('description')` constant (not `Symbol.for()`, which creates globally-shared symbols) and use it as the property key. Compute and attach such metadata at parse/load time so downstream writers can access it without a redundant file read. Add a brief inline comment noting that `JSON.stringify` silently omits symbol-keyed properties, as this serialization behavior is not universally known.

Avoid combining an existence check with a side-effecting operation in a single conditional expression. Separate them into distinct statements—first check, then act—so each step is independently readable and the side effect cannot be accidentally triggered as part of predicate evaluation.

When writing a comment that explains why an error is suppressed or treated as non-fatal, name the exact error type (e.g., `AbortError`) rather than using vague language like 'any errors' with a parenthetical example. Precision helps future maintainers know whether new error types should also be covered.

When introducing a custom helper type in a documentation snippet (e.g., under `docs/_snippets/`, to extend component props with additional story args), add a short comment directly above the type explaining its purpose and clearly stating whether it is optional for readers implementing the pattern in their own code.

When adding a callout or warning about a cross-cutting behavior (e.g., a builder quirk that affects build output), verify the note appears on every related documentation page—both the configuration API reference page and the corresponding integration or how-to guide—so the caveat is not buried in only one location.

When Storybook documentation recommends setting a Vite configuration option, specify that the setting must be applied through the `viteFinal` hook in `.storybook/main.ts` rather than referencing the Vite option in isolation; include an inline code snippet (e.g., `async viteFinal(config) { config.publicDir = false; return config; }`) or a link to Storybook's Vite builder documentation so readers know exactly where and how to apply the change.

When a utility is copied into a package because the original cannot be imported across a package boundary (e.g., the preview-to-manager boundary in addon-docs), add a `/** */` JSDoc block on the copy that explains: why it is duplicated, how it differs from the canonical version (e.g., only returns a preview URL rather than `{ managerHref, previewHref }`), and where the canonical version lives.

When calling `stringify` from `picoquery` in manager-api or router code, align the serialization options with the canonical usage in `code/core/src/router/utils.ts` (at minimum `nesting: true` and `nestingSyntax: 'js'`); document any intentional deviation from those defaults.

Do not leave test cases permanently disabled with `test.skip()` without an accompanying tracking issue or TODO that includes a resolution plan; error and exception branches (e.g., catch blocks and cross-origin fallback paths) must have dedicated test coverage.

When extracting a component ID from a story ID, do not split on `'--'` manually (e.g., `storyId.split('--')[0]`). Check whether `storybook/internal/csf` already provides a helper for story/component ID manipulation and use it instead.

Storybook tag strings such as `'autodocs'`, `'test'`, `'dev'`, `'manifest'`, `'attached-mdx'`, `'unattached-mdx'`, `'play-fn'`, and `'test-fn'` must be referenced via the canonical `Tag` object (defined in `code/core/src/shared/constants/tags.ts`, re-exported from `storybook/internal/core-server` for server/node code and from `storybook/manager-api` for manager/browser code). Raw string literals for these values are not acceptable anywhere in the codebase, including renderer packages such as `code/renderers/react/`.

`code/core/src/manager/globals/exports.ts` is auto-generated by `code/core/scripts/generate-source-files.ts`. Do not manually add or remove entries from this file; instead run the generator script so it discovers new exports (e.g., from `storybook/manager-api/index.ts`) automatically. Manual edits will be overwritten the next time the generator runs.

Avoid CSS selector overrides in a parent/wrapper styled component that target internals of a child component (e.g., `table { backgroundColor: ... }` inside a wrapper div). Components should accept styling customization only through explicit APIs such as props or a `className` prop. If the child component lacks the necessary API for context-specific styling, extend the child component with that API rather than reaching into it with an ancestor selector. When a styling fix is correct for all usages of a component (not just one specific consumer), apply the change in the component's own definition rather than as a context-specific override in a single consumer.

When adding or modifying entries in `sandbox-templates.ts` to enable a Storybook configuration option for CI coverage, check whether the option is supported by both Webpack and Vite builders; if it is, add sandbox entries for both builder types rather than only one. If only one builder supports the option, add a comment explaining why the other is omitted.
Performance Issue: When filtering a collection based on membership in another collection, pre-compute a `Set` of lookup values outside the loop or `.filter()` callback (e.g., `const ids = new Set(items.map(x => x.id))`) and use `Set.has()` for O(1) membership checks, rather than calling `.some()` or `.includes()` inside the callback, which results in O(n×m) complexity.
Code Style: Proofread prose in documentation, MIGRATION.md, release-note JSON entries (`docs/versions/`), source-code comments (inline comments, JSDoc blocks, config file comments), and descriptive lists for grammar errors (e.g., possessive 'its' vs. contraction 'it’s', correct plural/verb agreement like 'these props have been removed' not 'these prop has been removed'), common misspellings (e.g., 'superceded' → 'superseded'), stray editing artifacts (e.g., 'Thed' → 'The'), and grammatical parallelism (e.g., use 'well-maintained' rather than bare past participles in a list of adjectives).

In YAML code snippets within documentation (e.g., GitHub Actions workflow examples under `docs/_snippets/`), separate each top-level key (`name`, `on`, `permissions`, `concurrency`, `jobs`, etc.) with a blank line, and add blank lines between major sub-blocks within a job definition (e.g., between `environment` and `steps`) for readability.

In markdown files, bare URLs (e.g., `http://localhost:6006/`) must be wrapped in markdown link syntax (`[http://localhost:6006/](http://localhost:6006/)`) or enclosed in backtick code formatting. Bare URLs trigger markdownlint rule MD034 (no-bare-urls), which is enforced in this project's linting pipeline.

When adding a TypeScript type alias to a documentation snippet file (e.g., under `docs/_snippets/`), format it using multi-line syntax—one member per line with a trailing semicolon after the closing brace—to stay consistent with the style of existing type definitions in that directory.
